meta.title: Who originally recorded "Tennessee Waltz"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Patti Page's 1950 smash was a cover. Pee Wee King and His Golden West Cowboys released "Tennessee Waltz" first, on RCA Victor in January 1948 - and Cowboy Copas had recorded it even earlier, in April 1947.
meta.ogDescription: Not Patti Page. Pee Wee King and His Golden West Cowboys had the first release, RCA Victor, January 1948, a No. 3 country hit - and Cowboy Copas cut an earlier version in April 1947.

answer.label: Not a Patti Page original — a 1948 Pee Wee King and His Golden West Cowboys single on RCA Victor
answer.originalArtist: Pee Wee King and His Golden West Cowboys
answer.originalArtistDates: Pee Wee King, 1914–2000 · American country bandleader and songwriter; the Golden West Cowboys were his Grand Ole Opry band
answer.sourceLine: Patti Page’s 1950 record is so total a possession of this song that most people assume she introduced it. She did not. “Tennessee Waltz” was written in 1946 by bandleader Pee Wee King and his singer Redd Stewart, and King’s Golden West Cowboys cut it on 2 December 1947 at RCA Victor’s Chicago studio; RCA Victor issued it as single 20-2680 on 26 January 1948 — the first released recording — and it reached No. 3 country. The earliest recording is older still, and it is not King’s: Cowboy Copas, a former Golden West Cowboy, taped the song for King Records in Cincinnati in April 1947, but the label sat on it until March 1948. Page’s Mercury version arrived in November 1950 and spent nine weeks at No. 1 on the pop chart — and both country records have been standing in its shadow ever since.

original.heading: Who released it first
original.artist: Pee Wee King and His Golden West Cowboys
original.label: RCA Victor
original.released: Recorded 2 December 1947 at RCA Victor Studio A in Chicago and issued as a 78 rpm single, RCA Victor 20-2680, on 26 January 1948, credited to Pee Wee King and His Golden West Cowboys. That is the first released recording of the song — but not the first one made: Cowboy Copas had cut it for King Records in April 1947, and King held the master back until March 1948.
original.charted: Reached No. 3 on the Billboard country chart in 1948, selling roughly 300,000 copies.
original.writer: Pee Wee King and Redd Stewart
original.cover: Patti Page’s Mercury version (catalogue 5534) appeared in November 1950 as the flip side of “Boogie Woogie Santa Claus,” hit No. 1 on the Billboard pop chart on 30 December 1950 and stayed nine weeks, selling 2.3 million copies by May 1951.

trail: The 1948 single is catalogued as Victor 20-2680, and a transfer of the shellac itself is preserved at the Internet Archive ↗.
Wikipedia’s article on the song ↗ gives the 2 December 1947 session, the 26 January 1948 release, and the No. 3 country placing.

Released first is not the same as recorded first, and on this song they are different acts. The same Wikipedia entry ↗ says only that Cowboy Copas’s version was released by King Records (King 696) in March 1948, reaching No. 6 country. The session itself was far earlier: Honking Duck ↗ dates the King 696A master (matrix K2440) to 1 April 1947, and Praguefrank’s Cowboy Copas discography ↗ places the session at the King Recording Studio on Brewster Avenue, Cincinnati, in April 1947 — eight months before the Golden West Cowboys went into RCA’s Chicago studio.
The composition, registered by Acuff-Rose in February 1948, is credited on MusicBrainz ↗ to Pee Wee King as composer and Redd Stewart as lyricist.

authors.name: Pee Wee King and His Golden West Cowboys
authors.heading: Pee Wee King and His Golden West Cowboys
authors.metaLine: Pee Wee King, 1914–2000 · American country bandleader · recorded 2 December 1947, released January 1948 on RCA Victor
authors.bio: Born Julius Frank Anthony Kuczynski in Abrams, Wisconsin, Pee Wee King led the Golden West Cowboys, one of the most stylistically adventurous bands ever to work the Grand Ole Opry — he pushed waltzes, polkas and cowboy material into country music, and his band brought stage dancing and rhinestone tailoring to the Opry stage. He wrote or co-wrote more than 400 songs and cut more than 150 singles. His Golden West Cowboys recorded “Tennessee Waltz” on 2 December 1947 for RCA Victor; the single reached No. 3 on the country chart and sold some 300,000 copies. King was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 1974.

authors.name: Patti Page
authors.heading: Patti Page
authors.metaLine: 1927–2013 · American pop singer · Mercury single, November 1950 · nine weeks at No. 1
authors.bio: Clara Ann Fowler of Claremore, Oklahoma became the top-charting female vocalist of the 1950s and one of the first pop artists to harmonise with herself on record, via engineer Bill Putnam’s overdubbing. Her “Tennessee Waltz” reached her almost by accident: Billboard reviewer Jerry Wexler heard an R&B version by Erskine Hawkins and suggested the song to Page’s manager Jack Rael, and it was cut in a hurry as the flip of a Christmas novelty. It spent nine weeks at No. 1 and became one of the best-selling singles of the century. Nothing about that record is a mistake — only the chronology people attach to it.

authors.name: Pee Wee King and Redd Stewart
authors.heading: Pee Wee King & Redd Stewart
authors.metaLine: Pee Wee King, 1914–2000 · Redd Stewart, 1923–2003 · written 1946 · published by Acuff-Rose Music
authors.bio: King and Stewart wrote “Tennessee Waltz” in 1946, on the road to Nashville, after hearing Bill Monroe’s “Kentucky Waltz” and deciding their own state deserved one. Henry Ellis “Redd” Stewart, born in Ashland City, Tennessee, had joined the Golden West Cowboys in 1937 and became the band’s lead singer after Eddy Arnold went solo; he also wrote “Soldier’s Last Letter,” a 1944 hit for Ernest Tubb, and co-wrote “You Belong to Me” with King. They also made the first released recording of their own song — though not the first recording of it: Cowboy Copas, who had sung with the Golden West Cowboys himself, got the song onto tape in April 1947, eight months before its writers did.

misattribution.heading: Right song, wrong beginning
misattribution.intro: Patti Page’s record is one of the best-selling singles of the twentieth century, which is exactly why it is mistaken for the first one. Here is the order things actually happened in.

items.who: Patti Page originated “Tennessee Waltz” with her 1950 Mercury single.
items.why: Her version spent nine weeks at No. 1 on the pop chart and had sold 2.3 million copies by May 1951, dwarfing everything that came before it in the mainstream market.

items.who: Cowboy Copas, cut at the King Recording Studio in Cincinnati in April 1947 (King 696A, matrix K2440), but not released until March 1948.
items.why: Copas, a former Golden West Cowboy, taped the song eight months before its writers did — the discographies of the King sessions date the master to April 1947 — and his record still reached No. 6 country and sold about 80,000 copies once King finally issued it.

items.who: Pee Wee King and His Golden West Cowboys, recorded 2 December 1947, released by RCA Victor as 20-2680 on 26 January 1948.
items.why: King’s single was the first version the public could buy, two months ahead of the Copas record. It reached No. 3 on the country chart and sold around 300,000 copies — a substantial country hit that never reached the pop audience Page later did.

items.who: Pee Wee King (music) and Redd Stewart (lyrics), written in 1946.
items.why: The writers made the first released record themselves — King led the band, Stewart was its lead singer — but even they were not the first into a studio with it.

misattribution.truthLine: The first released recording is Pee Wee King and His Golden West Cowboys’, cut 2 December 1947 and issued by RCA Victor on 26 January 1948. The earliest recording of all is Cowboy Copas’s, made in April 1947 but held back until March 1948. Patti Page’s version came in November 1950.

context.heading: Why the cover swallowed the original
lead: The interesting question is not why Patti Page had a hit — it is why a record that had already been a country hit twice could be treated, in 1950, as brand new. The answer is that in the late 1940s the country chart and the pop chart described two more or less sealed markets. Pee Wee King’s RCA Victor single went to No. 3 country in 1948 and Cowboy Copas’s King Records version — recorded eight months before King’s but held back until March 1948 — followed it to No. 6, but neither crossed into the pop audience that bought Mercury singles.

The bridge was accidental. Billboard reviewer Jerry Wexler — years before Atlantic Records made him famous — heard an R&B version by Erskine Hawkins in October 1950 and passed the song to Page’s manager Jack Rael. Page cut it fast, without a proper arrangement, as the B-side of a Christmas novelty. The novelty is forgotten; the flip side spent nine weeks at No. 1 and sold in the millions. When a record outsells its predecessors by that margin, the public files it as the beginning of the story.
detailsBody: 1946 — Pee Wee King and Redd Stewart write “Tennessee Waltz,” prompted by Bill Monroe’s “Kentucky Waltz.”
April 1947 — Cowboy Copas, a former Golden West Cowboy, records the song at the King Recording Studio in Cincinnati. It is the earliest known recording, and King Records leaves it on the shelf.
2 December 1947 — Pee Wee King and His Golden West Cowboys record it at RCA Victor Studio A in Chicago.

26 January 1948 — RCA Victor issues the single as Victor 20-2680, with “Tennessee Waltz” on the B-side of “Rootie Tootie”; it is the first release of the song, reaches No. 3 on the country chart and sells about 300,000 copies.
26 February 1948 — the composition is registered by Acuff-Rose Publications of Nashville.
March 1948 — King Records finally issues the Copas recording as King 696; it reaches No. 6 country.
October 1950 — Billboard’s Jerry Wexler reviews an Erskine Hawkins R&B version and recommends the song to Patti Page’s manager, Jack Rael.
November 1950 — Page’s Mercury single (catalogue 5534) appears with “Tennessee Waltz” as the flip of “Boogie Woogie Santa Claus.”
30 December 1950 — Page’s version reaches No. 1 on the Billboard pop chart, where it stays for nine weeks; it had sold 2.3 million copies by May 1951.
1965 — Tennessee adopts the song as an official state song by Senate Joint Resolution 9.
context.pull: The song was a country hit twice before America heard it.

schema.faqAnswer: No. "Tennessee Waltz" was written in 1946 by Pee Wee King and Redd Stewart, and the first released recording is theirs: Pee Wee King and His Golden West Cowboys recorded it on 2 December 1947 and RCA Victor issued it as 20-2680 on 26 January 1948. listenCover.what: Patti Page’s Mercury recording of late 1950, the multi-tracked vocal that sold in the millions and became the version everyone knows.
listenCover.source: Auto-generated upload on the “Patti Page - Topic” channel, description line “Provided to YouTube by Universal Music Group” (UMG holds the Mercury catalogue), phonogram line “℗ 1950 UMG Recordings, Inc.” — the 1950 phonogram year is what rules out a later remake, since a re-cut would carry its own year. TWO DISCREPANCIES I should flag rather than bury: (1) the “Released on” field is 1960-09-07, i.e. the file is delivered from the 1960 Mercury compilation Golden Hits, and sources conflict on whether that LP used the original masters or 1960 Nashville re-recordings — the ℗ 1950 line is my basis for concluding it is the original master; (2) runtime is 185s against a MusicBrainz cluster for Patti Page’s Tennessee Waltz of 176000–179666ms for most entries, so it sits about 5s long, at the outer end of tolerance though within the ~15s allowance (MusicBrainz also carries 183600ms and 186000ms entries that match it closely). The other two Topic uploads were worse: aV160VUJqnY is ℗ 2005 DRG (a genuine later re-recording) and AMDhFjjC5LA is a 2015 Orchard compilation.
